title: SELinux — Labels, Booleans, AVC
lead: SELinux gives every file and process a label. When a service fails, the culprit is often a wrong label; learn to find the cause instead of switching SELinux off.
objectives: You read the SELinux modes (enforcing, permissive, disabled) and explain why disabling it permanently is a bad idea.
You read file labels with `ls -Z` and fix them persistently with `chcon`, `semanage fcontext` and `restorecon`.
You manage booleans with `getsebool` and `setsebool -P` and resolve AVC denials with `ausearch` and `sealert`.
You read the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent, AppArmor, with `aa-status` and tell complain from enforce mode.

sections.title: What SELinux is, modes
body: Classic permissions (rwx) look at the owner. **SELinux** is an extra layer: every process and file has a **label (context)** and the policy says which label may do what to which. A label looks like `user:role:type:level`; the **type** field matters most in daily work (e.g. `httpd_t`, `httpd_sys_content_t`).

There are three modes: **enforcing** (violations are blocked and logged), **permissive** (only logged, not blocked; for debugging) and **disabled** (off). RHEL/Rocky/Alma default to enforcing. Debian/Ubuntu use **AppArmor** instead.

commands.what: Prints the running SELinux mode.
commands.where: First check when a service misbehaves.
commands.why: Narrows down whether SELinux is involved.

commands.what: Shows mode, policy type and the mode in the config file.
commands.where: When you need a general summary.
commands.why: You see the difference between running and persistent mode.

commands.what: Switches to permissive for now (resets on reboot).
commands.where: To test temporarily whether SELinux is the cause.
commands.why: If the problem vanishes in permissive, SELinux is the culprit; turn it back on with `setenforce 1`.

commands.what: File holding the persistent mode (`SELINUX=enforcing`).
commands.where: When setting the mode persistently across reboots.
commands.why: If you write `disabled`, labels go stale and re-enabling needs a long relabel.

sections.tip: Troubleshooting order: `getenforce`, test with `setenforce 0`, read the log, fix, then `setenforce 1`.
sections.warn: Do not make `setenforce 0` or `SELINUX=disabled` a habit. Use permissive for a temporary test and the right label or boolean for a lasting fix.

sections.title: Labels: ls -Z, chcon, semanage, restorecon
body: `ls -Z` shows a file's label. The web server (`httpd_t`) can only read web-typed files such as `httpd_sys_content_t`. If you `mv` a file from your home directory, it keeps the old `user_home_t` label and access is denied.

`chcon` changes the label immediately but **not persistently**: `restorecon` or a relabel wipes it. The lasting way has two steps: first write the rule into the policy with `semanage fcontext`, then apply it with `restorecon`.

commands.what: Lists the SELinux label of files.
commands.where: When looking at the file type after a denial.
commands.why: You compare the expected type with the actual type.

commands.what: Changes a file's type temporarily.
commands.where: For quick experiments.
commands.why: Proves the label fixes the problem; but it is not persistent.

commands.what: Adds a persistent labeling rule for a path pattern.
commands.where: When using a non-standard directory (e.g. /srv/web).
commands.why: The rule stays in the policy and survives a relabel.

commands.what: Restores labels to what the policy says (-R recursive, -v verbose).
commands.where: After `semanage fcontext` or after moving files.
commands.why: Applies the rule to the real files.

sections.tip: A file copied with `cp` takes the label of the target directory; a file moved with `mv` keeps its old label. Run `restorecon` after moving.
sections.warn: Do not run `restorecon -R /` or other huge paths; it takes long and can surprise you. Look first with `-n` (dry run).

sections.title: Booleans
body: Switches that turn common behaviors on and off without rewriting the policy are called **booleans**: `httpd_can_network_connect` lets the web server connect to the network, `httpd_enable_homedirs` opens home directories.
`setsebool` alone changes the **running** state and is lost on reboot. Add `-P` to make it persistent. Enable only what you need; every boolean is a hole in the wall.

commands.what: Lists all booleans and their states.
commands.where: When searching for the right switch (`| grep httpd`).
commands.why: The right boolean saves you from fiddling with labels.

commands.what: Shows the state of one boolean.
commands.where: To verify before and after a change.
commands.why: You see that the change took effect.

commands.what: Turns a boolean on/off persistently.
commands.where: When a service must reach the network or home directories.
commands.why: Without `-P` the setting is lost on reboot.

commands.what: Lists booleans with descriptions and persistent/running state.
commands.where: To learn what a boolean does.
commands.why: The description keeps you from enabling the wrong switch.

sections.tip: A new port may need more than a boolean: add it to the service type with `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`.
sections.warn: Pick the narrowest boolean; broad switches like `httpd_unified` grant a lot.

sections.title: AVC denials: ausearch, sealert, audit.log
body: When SELinux blocks something, an **AVC** (Access Vector Cache) record lands in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. It has the source label (`scontext`), target label (`tcontext`), class (`tclass`) and the blocked permission (`{ read }`). If `permissive=1`, the access was not blocked, only logged.

Reading order: who (`comm`, `scontext`), what (`name`, `tcontext`), what it tried to do (`{ ... }`). Then fix: wrong label means `restorecon`, a behavior permission means a boolean, a new port means `semanage port`. Generating a module with `audit2allow` is the last resort.

commands.what: Searches the audit log for recent AVC records.
commands.where: Right after a denial.
commands.why: Finds the relevant records without wading through the raw log.

commands.what: Analyzes the log and suggests a fix (setroubleshoot package).
commands.where: When you want a cause and fix summary.
commands.why: Often suggests the right `restorecon` or `setsebool` command.

commands.what: Filters AVC lines in the audit log.
commands.where: Without ausearch or when inspecting a log copy.
commands.why: The simplest method that works everywhere.

commands.what: Counts denied records.
commands.where: To measure the size of the problem.
commands.why: Tells you whether it is one repeated denial or many sources.

sections.tip: Without auditd, records may appear in `journalctl -t setroubleshoot` or `dmesg`.
sections.warn: Do not load a module with `audit2allow -M` for every AVC. Try the label and the boolean first; a module can grant needlessly broad access.

sections.title: Debian/Ubuntu: AppArmor
body: Ubuntu and Debian use **AppArmor** instead of SELinux. Instead of labels, each program has a **path-based profile**. A profile can be in **enforce** mode (rules applied) or **complain** mode (only logs, like permissive in SELinux).

The logic is the same: read the status, put a profile in complain if needed, see in the log what was blocked, fix the profile and set enforce again. Denials show up in `/var/log/syslog` or `journalctl` as `apparmor="DENIED"`.

commands.what: Lists loaded profiles and their modes (enforce/complain).
commands.where: For a status check.
commands.why: You see which programs are confined.

commands.what: Puts a profile in complain mode.
commands.where: When a profile blocks something, for a temporary test.
commands.why: Logs without blocking; you see what is needed.

commands.what: Returns a profile to enforce mode.
commands.where: After the test is done.
commands.why: Protection is active again.

commands.what: Filters AppArmor denial lines in the log.
commands.where: When inspecting a denial.
commands.why: Shows which path was blocked.

sections.tip: Rocky vs Ubuntu: `getenforce` is like `aa-status`, `setenforce 0` is like `aa-complain`, `setenforce 1` is like `aa-enforce`.
sections.danger: Turning a profile off with `aa-disable` or setting SELinux permanently disabled removes a security layer. Find the cause with complain/permissive instead.

t01.text: Read the persistent SELinux mode with `cat ~/lab/selinux_config`.

t02.text: Count the denied records in the audit log with `grep -c denied ~/lab/audit.log`.

t03.text: List the httpd booleans with `grep httpd ~/lab/booleans.txt`.
t03.hint: The file has the form `name --> state`.

t04.text: Change into the lab directory with `cd ~/lab`.
t04.hint: Later tasks then need no path.

t05.text: The label in `context.txt` is `user:role:type:level`. Print the **type** field with `cut -d: -f3 context.txt`.
t05.hint: Delimiter is a colon, type is field three. Be in the lab directory first.

t06.text: Write only the httpd records to `httpd_denials.txt` with `grep 'comm="httpd"' audit.log > httpd_denials.txt`.
t06.hint: Single quotes around a pattern with double quotes; > redirects output to a file.

t07.text: Find the AppArmor line in complain mode with `grep complain aa_status.txt`.
t07.hint: You expect a line with 'complain mode'.

t08.text: Predict: how many records in `audit.log` have `permissive=1` (not blocked)? Then verify with `grep -c permissive=1 audit.log`.
t08.hint: Look at the permissive value at the end of each line.

t09.text: Predict: how many booleans in `booleans.txt` are off? Then verify with `grep -c ' off$' booleans.txt`.
t09.hint: $ marks the end of the line.

t10.text: Debug: `broken_config` has `SELINUX=disabled`. Rewrite the file so it has `SELINUX=enforcing` and `SELINUXTYPE=targeted`.

t11.text: Debug: `runbook.sh` uses `setenforce 0` and does not make the boolean persistent. Rewrite it with the single line `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on`.

t12.text: Mini project: write a script `fix_web.sh`. Line 1: `semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/web(/.*)?"`, line 2: `restorecon -Rv /srv/web`. Then make it executable with `chmod 755`.
t12.hint: Use `>` for the first line and `>>` for the second.

t13.text: Mini project: run `cut -d' ' -f10 audit.log | sort | uniq -c > top_comm.txt` to write how often each program was denied into `top_comm.txt`.

t14.text: Challenge: write the lines of `webfiles.txt` that do not have the web type (`httpd_sys_content_t`) to `wrong_labels.txt`.

t15.text: Challenge: write the booleans in `booleans.txt` that are on to `booleans_on.txt`.

t16.text: Ticket: The website returns 403. After checking `webfiles.txt` and `audit.log`: `about.html` has the `user_home_t` label. Write a one-line note in `ticket.txt`: wrong type `user_home_t`, correct type `httpd_sys_content_t`, fix `restorecon`.

t17.text: Ticket: The web app cannot connect to port 8888; the log shows `name_connect` and `unreserved_port_t`. Write this command into `fix_port.sh`: `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`.
t17.hint: Write the command with `echo` in single quotes and redirect with `>`.

vm.intro: Do this part on a Rocky/Alma VM (SELinux ships there). On Ubuntu go to v06. Before anything else take a **VM snapshot** (module 0.2). Work in a fresh lab, not on a live server.

v01.title: Read the mode
v01.text: Find the running and persistent SELinux mode. Do not change the mode in this task.
differs: If you get `command not found`, you are on Ubuntu; go to v06.
If it says `Disabled`, SELinux is off in the VM; use a Rocky/Alma image.

v02.title: See the labels
v02.text: Read file and process labels. Compare the web content directory and your home directory.
differs: If `/var/www` is missing, httpd is not installed; install with `sudo dnf install -y httpd` and retry.

v03.title: Persistent label rule
v03.text: Define and apply a persistent label for a non-standard directory. Make sure you took a snapshot first; work only in this test directory.

blocks.cmd:
sudo mkdir -p /srv/web
echo hello | sudo tee /srv/web/index.html
ls -Zd /srv/web/index.html
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/web(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/web
ls -Zd /srv/web/index.html

differs: If `semanage: command not found`, run `sudo dnf install -y policycoreutils-python-utils`.
If the rule already exists, use `-m` instead of `-a`.

v04.title: Change a boolean
v04.text: Read a boolean, turn it on persistently and verify. Restore the old value at the end.

blocks.cmd:
getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect off

differs: `-P` can be slow (policy is rebuilt); wait a minute.
If the boolean is not found, search with `getsebool -a | grep httpd`.

v05.title: Find an AVC record
v05.text: Search the audit log for denials. If there are none, that is fine; breaking a label on purpose to produce one is optional.

blocks.cmd:
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent
sudo grep -c AVC /var/log/audit/audit.log
sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log | head -20

differs: `<no matches>` is normal on a clean system.
If `sealert` is missing, run `sudo dnf install -y setroubleshoot-server`.

v06.title: AppArmor (Ubuntu)
v06.text: On an Ubuntu/Debian VM read the AppArmor status. Do not change profile modes (optional: `aa-complain` then `aa-enforce`).

blocks.cmd:
sudo aa-status | head -15
sudo apparmor_status | head -3
blocks.expected:
apparmor module is loaded.
12 profiles are loaded.

differs: If `aa-status: command not found`, run `sudo apt install -y apparmor-utils`.
Rocky has no AppArmor; v01-v05 are your tasks.

q1.q: A service fails because of SELinux. What is the best first diagnostic step?
options: See the mode with `getenforce`, test with temporary `setenforce 0`, then read the log
q1.explain: First determine the mode and whether SELinux is the cause using temporary permissive, then find the reason in the AVC log. Disabling permanently removes the security layer.

q2.q: You want the label of `/srv/web` to survive a relabel. Which is the right way?
q2.explain: `chcon` is not persistent. `semanage fcontext` writes the rule into the policy and `restorecon` applies it to the files.

q3.q: You ran `setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on` and after a reboot it was gone. Why?
options: There was no `-P` flag, so the setting only lived in the running system
The boolean was a non-existent switch
q3.explain: `-P` makes the setting persistent. Without it the change only applies to the running system.

q4.q: On Ubuntu, how do you make a profile only log for now?
q4.explain: In AppArmor, `aa-complain` makes a profile only log, like permissive in SELinux; `aa-enforce` brings it back.

summary: SELinux works with labels; the main field is the type (`httpd_t`, `httpd_sys_content_t`).
Modes: enforcing, permissive, disabled. Use `setenforce 0` for tests, never disable permanently.
Labels: read with `ls -Z`, fix persistently with `semanage fcontext` + `restorecon`; `chcon` is not persistent.
Booleans: `getsebool`, persistent with `setsebool -P`; for a new port use `semanage port`.
AVC: `ausearch -m AVC`, `sealert -a`, `audit.log`; read who, what, what it tried to do.

glossary.meaning: Label-based mandatory access control (MAC); an extra layer on top of classic permissions.
Security label shaped `user:role:type:level`; the type is the key field.
The label field the policy writes rules for, e.g. `httpd_sys_content_t`.
Mode that blocks and logs violations.
Debug mode that only logs violations without blocking.
Policy switch for a common behavior; persistent with `-P`.
Access Vector Cache; the audit log record of an SELinux denial.
Command that restores a file label to what the policy rule says.
Path-based profile system on Debian/Ubuntu; has enforce and complain modes.
